units.title: Digestion & metabolism
units.subtitle: Follow a meal from molecules to cells.
objectives: Distinguish mechanical digestion, chemical digestion, and absorption.
Trace carbohydrates, proteins, and fats through digestion and transport.
Predict how enzymes, pH, and changes to anatomy affect digestion.
guide: Mechanical digestion increases exposed surface area; chemical digestion breaks molecular bonds. Absorption moves products across the intestinal epithelium.
Amylase acts on starch, proteases on proteins, and lipases on fats. Enzyme activity depends on conditions including pH.
Most absorbed sugars and amino acids enter villus capillaries and travel toward the liver through the hepatic portal system. Most long-chain dietary fat travels initially through lacteals.
Use the coffee-with-cream example to trace each nutrient separately. For surgery questions, identify what organ function is changed before predicting the effect.

units.title: Kidneys & urine
units.subtitle: Connect filtration to the evidence in a sample.
objectives: Trace blood and filtrate through the kidney.
Distinguish filtration, reabsorption, secretion, and excretion.
Connect glomerular injury and hormonal regulation to urine findings.
guide: Filtration moves fluid from glomerular blood into the capsule. Reabsorption returns substances from tubular fluid to blood; secretion moves substances the other way.
The afferent arteriole supplies the glomerulus, and the efferent arteriole drains it. Filtration depends on pressures and the barrier, not just systemic blood pressure.
A healthy barrier retains cells and most large proteins. Persistent urinary albumin can indicate barrier damage.
Interpret case findings together. A urine result is evidence to explain physiologically, not a diagnosis by itself.

units.title: Fluids & acid–base
units.subtitle: Explain where water goes and what controls pH.
objectives: Predict cell volume changes from tonicity.
Distinguish intracellular, interstitial, and plasma compartments.
Explain buffering, ventilation, and kidney contributions to pH.
guide: Intracellular fluid is inside cells. Extracellular fluid includes plasma and interstitial fluid; water crosses between compartments.
Tonicity depends on effectively nonpenetrating solutes. Water enters cells in hypotonic surroundings and leaves cells in hypertonic surroundings.
Buffers resist pH change. Ventilation adjusts carbon dioxide; kidneys regulate hydrogen-ion excretion and bicarbonate handling.
Use the egg-osmosis experiment to explain mass changes. Use the exhaled-carbon-dioxide experiment to connect ventilation to acid–base chemistry.

units.title: Hormones & feedback
units.subtitle: Reason through the signal, receptor, and response.
objectives: Relate hormone solubility to receptor location and action.
Interpret experimental changes in endocrine organs.
guide: A hormone can circulate widely, but only cells with suitable receptors respond directly.
Many water-soluble hormones bind surface receptors and signal through intracellular pathways. Steroid hormones commonly bind intracellular receptors and alter gene expression.
In negative feedback, rising target-gland hormone usually reduces upstream stimulation. Distinguish the hormone injected from the organ that normally produces it.
For mystery-hormone experiments, compare the treated group with a control, then explain changes at every step of the axis.

units.title: Lymph & immunity
units.subtitle: Trace the route from a barrier to immune memory.
objectives: Trace lymph return and identify lymphatic organ functions.
Explain antigen specificity, vaccination, and autoimmunity.
guide: Lymphatic vessels return interstitial fluid to circulation; intestinal lacteals also transport absorbed dietary lipids.
Innate defenses include barriers, phagocytes, natural killer cells, and inflammation. Adaptive responses involve antigen-specific B and T lymphocytes.
Activated B cells can become antibody-secreting plasma cells. Memory cells support faster responses on later encounters.
Distinguish the spleen, which filters blood, from lymph nodes, which filter lymph. Use mechanisms rather than symptoms alone when explaining autoimmune cases.

units.title: Reproduction & development
units.subtitle: Connect anatomy, hormone cycles, and fertilization.
objectives: Relate hormone feedback to ovulation and contraception.
Explain fertilization, early development, and childbirth feedback.
guide: Spermatogenesis occurs in seminiferous tubules. Sertoli (nurse) cells support developing germ cells; Leydig cells produce testosterone.
FSH supports follicular development. Sustained high estradiol near midcycle can produce positive feedback and the LH surge.
After ovulation, the corpus luteum produces progesterone and estrogen. Falling hormone support contributes to endometrial shedding if pregnancy does not occur.
Connect the ovarian cycle to IVF reasoning, and connect oxytocin-driven contractions to positive feedback during birth.
